item.title: 🧼 FUGA DE PELÍCULA: LOS ATRAPARON EN BOLIVIA Walter Ernesto Medina, de 29 años y nacionalidad dominicana, y Jaime Olmos Delgadillo, de 36 y nacionalidad boliviana, protagonizaron una fuga insólita en La Quiaca. Ambos estaban detenidos en una dependencia de Gendarmería Nacional y habrían utilizado detergente o jabón líquido para deslizarse entre las rejas y escapar. Por el momento, las autoridades no confirmaron qué sustancia usaron. La fuga activó un operativo de búsqueda y los dos hombres lograron cruzar hacia Bolivia. Sin embargo, las autoridades bolivianas los localizaron y los entregaron nuevamente a la Argentina a través del puente internacional que une Villazón con La Quiaca. La secuencia quedó registrada por cámaras de seguridad. Los dos detenidos volvieron a quedar bajo custodia argentina y deberán continuar con sus procesos judiciales. Ahora, los investigadores buscan establecer cómo lograron escapar y qué fallas de seguridad les permitieron abandonar el lugar sin que los efectivos advirtieran la maniobra a tiempo. ▶️Seguí el minuto a minuto de todas las noticias en nuestro canal de YouTube. #LaQuiaca #Fuga #Policiales #Insolito | Crónica TV

item.title: Satellites accurately detect methane emissions in largest controlled test yet
item.description: Researchers have conducted the largest-ever controlled test of space-based methane monitoring, finding that dedicated methane sensors correctly detected nearly all methane plumes released on clear days. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The stubby legs of ancient sled dogs helped people traverse the Arctic for the past 9,000 years
item.description: For centuries, dogs have helped people travel across the Arctic, hauling supplies, equipment and other goods through snowy landscapes where other domesticated animals struggled to venture. Now, a new study publishing Oct. 14 in the journal iScience finds that sled dogs might have evolved shorter legs that helped them pull loads more efficiently. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sustained pressure halts cancer cell migration and triggers death in 3D lab models
item.description: The growth and death of cancer cells in the lab are studied primarily in two-dimensional cell cultures. In a study published in the journal Developmental Cell on Oct. 14, researchers instead used three-dimensional models to uncover how pressure and mechanical confinement impact cell growth—halting the cells' metastatic behavior and ultimately leading to their death. The findings could lead to the development of new biomarkers to predict which cancers are more likely to spread, or metastasize, and could ultimately lead to new approaches for preventing metastasis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robotic 'time crystal' organizes itself into a single rhythm despite random disturbances
item.description: Scientists have developed a material that can grow and coordinate its own movement until the entire structure pulses in unison, paving the way for versatile robots that behave more like living systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Microplastics are chemically active and could cause biological harm
item.description: Plastics are supposed to be chemically inert. It's the reason they're used so frequently to package food, bottle water and create children's toys: They're safe. But something important happens when a large piece of plastic fragments into micro- and nanoparticles. Its surface area increases dramatically relative to its volume. Vastly more of the material is now exposed to its surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Not all early birds evolved toward better flight, Jurassic fossil suggests
item.description: For early birds, evolution wasn't always about becoming better flyers. This conclusion is supported by the recent discovery of a remarkably well-preserved, 150-million-year-old bird fossil from Fujian province, China, which is challenging long-held assumptions about early bird evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Modeling study shows early tetrapods had surprisingly little ability to move their necks
item.description: A new model using sturgeon as a material analog has made it possible to estimate how the backbones of some of the first animals on land could and could not move. These results disprove a long-standing hypothesis that changes in early tetrapod anatomy as they moved onto land gave them improved neck mobility. The study, led by a researcher at Uppsala University, formerly of Carleton University in Canada, has been published in the journal Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-enhanced weather model doubles predictive power two to six weeks out
item.description: In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Little fish, big deal—Record haul of baby sturgeons offers hope for the future
item.description: Just a few centimeters long, slimy and covered in razor-sharp spines, baby sturgeons look like creatures from one of the Alien movies. But for the people who pull them from the river, these diminutive ugly ducklings of the fish world are a beautiful sight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Team builds resource-sharing technology platform for nonprofits
item.description: Nonprofit organizations have historically struggled with underfunding, scarce resources and even identifying what physical, human, social and financial capital they already have. But what if there were an easy way they could share surplus assets with other social enterprises to make better use of their collective resources and increase their community impact? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could a molecular ZIP code unlock treatments for untreatable diseases?
item.description: Imagine a medicine that stops seizures at their source, switches off instructions that keep a cancerous tumor growing and prevents Alzheimer's from stealing memories and wreaking havoc on the brain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 35% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
item.description: Berkshire's latest investment follows the $600 million it invested in the company's IPO this July. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: How shark ecotourism sparks long-term conservation
item.description: People who join shark ecotourism tours are more likely to take action to protect sharks, including donating to related causes, signing petitions or speaking up online, new research from the University of Sydney shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: DNA analysis uncovers first known genetic connection between rare New Caledonian plant and parasitic plant
item.description: A new genetic analysis tool developed by UF assistant professor of biology Liming Cai, Ph.D., has led to the discovery of the first known interaction between Amborella, a rare New Caledonian plant, and a parasitic plant called Hachettea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your dog may link sounds with shapes, just like you do
item.description: Sounds have shapes. That might sound strange since sound waves are invisible, but a famous psychological experiment in the 1920s showed that our brains naturally link spoken sounds to visual forms. According to new research published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, dogs may do this too. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemists develop blueprint for designing powerful fluorescent materials for better disease detection
item.description: The team, led by professors Simon Lewis and Tony James and Dr. Dan Pantos in the university's Department of Chemistry, has transformed azulene, a naturally occurring blue compound found in certain mushrooms and corals, into a versatile tool for biological imaging and chemical sensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
item.description: The consumer price index was expected to increase 0.6% in September on a monthly basis and 3.6% from a year ago, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: New evidence points to two feeding black holes just 175 parsecs apart lurking in the early universe
item.description: Astronomers have found two actively feeding supermassive black holes separated by just 175 parsecs (570 light-years) in a galaxy seen when the universe was only about 2 billion years old. The system, MG B2016+112, lies at a redshift of 3.273 and is the most compact dual AGN known at this redshift. The study was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 25. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How lessons from fisheries management could help us govern Earth's orbital space
item.description: The space industry is rapidly expanding. About 20,000 satellites already circle Earth, a number that could reach 100,000 by 2030. They bring growing environmental costs: space debris, collision risks, atmospheric pollution from launches and reentry and interference with astronomical observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA to Discuss Artemis Acceleration, Status of Upcoming Moon Missions
item.description: NASA will provide an update on its plans to return American astronauts to the surface of the Moon by 2028 at 2 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 23, at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Participants in the briefing include: The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Introduced species aren't good or bad—they are labeled according to human interests
item.description: In George Orwell's 1945 allegorical novella "Animal Farm," pigs coach the other revolutionary farm animals in their new creed of Animalism using the memorable maxim: four legs good, two legs bad. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Math under pressure may make a gamble's downside seem smaller
item.description: People who tackled arithmetic problems while stressed by a countdown clock, error buzzers and an observer nearby later gave potential losses less weight when deciding whether to accept a gamble. This finding from a new study suggests that pressure may change the balance between how people perceive what they could stand to gain and what they could lose. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's climate system increasingly unstable, but signs of positive change emerge
item.description: The seventh annual report by an international coalition led by Oregon State University scientists says the Earth's climate system is quickly becoming unstable and that while signs of important societal changes are emerging, greater and faster action is necessary. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study finds gendered messaging can backfire
item.description: Campaigns and initiatives aimed at advancing equity for girls and women often reference gender—"The future is female" or "Fight like a girl," for instance. However, is such messaging effective in championing their abilities and in inspiring others? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Lost' Iron Age cemetery reanalyzed more than 70 years after its finds went missing
item.description: In 1955, workers in a chalk quarry in Highsted, near Sittingbourne, were working when a human skull came tumbling down the bank at the edge of a pit. It would be the first of some 26 burials, all belonging to an ancient cemetery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronomical nanosatellite VERTECS completes initial operations and begins scientific observations
item.description: A research team from the Kyushu Institute of Technology, Kwansei Gakuin University, Tokyo City University, Kanazawa University, the University of Tokyo and other institutions has successfully completed the test operations conducted since the satellite was released into orbit. Having confirmed that the satellite meets its specified performance requirements, the team has begun routine operations for scientific astronomical observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
item.description: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
item.description: Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why the AI shopping revolution could backfire on retailers
item.description: Retailers have every reason to be interested in AI. A shopping assistant that answers questions at any hour, compares products instantly and offers personalized recommendations sounds like a win for customers and businesses alike. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
item.description: Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Children's mental health struggles may expose parents to stigma tied to parenting ideals
item.description: Parents of children with mental health problems may experience stigma when the ideals that matter most to being considered a "good parent" are perceived as not being met, according to preliminary research led by Weill Cornell Medicine, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons and NewYork-Presbyterian investigators. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
item.description: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study finds overlooked 'forever chemicals' widespread in New Jersey tap water and bottled beverages
item.description: Researchers at New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) have found that a largely overlooked class of "forever chemicals" is widespread in New Jersey drinking water and commercially available bottled beverages, raising new questions about how these persistent contaminants are monitored and potentially introduced into everyday products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum network test checks entanglement without having to trust detectors
item.description: Quantum networks are systems that connect different users or devices using principles of quantum mechanics. In the future, these networks could help improve the security of communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
item.description: Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
item.description: Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: El 13 de octubre de 2026, la imagen del día del NASA Earth Observatory fue una instantánea fascinante tomada por el satélite Landsat 9 desde el cielo de Australia. En ella se ve el cráter Araña ( Spider crater ), una deformación del terreno ubicada en la región de Kimberley, en Australia Occidental. Como su propio nombre indica, tiene una curiosa forma de araña que ha llamado la atención de los científicos desde hace años. item.title: Trailblazing technique uncovers real shape of scorching-hot exoplanet atmospheres
item.description: Until now, the alien white-hot worlds of exoplanets have been depicted as circular, but new research has revealed the true shape of their atmospheres to be a deformed sphere rather than a perfect circle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient climate shifts may explain why today's flowering plants are so diverse
item.description: The two warmest time periods on Earth in the past 140 million years drove both mass extinctions and explosions in plant diversity, according to researchers in Australia and Austria who say this could explain how flowering plants became dominant among land plants. The study, published in Nature Plants, examined fossilized pollen and spores to show that the mid-Cretaceous and early Cenozoic periods of extreme global warmth were central to plant evolution. This applies not only to flowering plants, but also to the other main land plant groups. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hemos detectado la ráfaga de radio más lejana jamás vista: salió de su galaxia hace más de 11.000 millones de años
item.description: Unos científicos de la Universidad de Northwestern han detectado la ráfaga rápida de radio (FRB por sus siglas en inglés) más lejana que se ha descrito jamás. Esto no es interesante solo por el récord que supone. También ha sido una gran noticia, porque aporta información muy útil sobre la galaxia de la que proviene y, de paso, da respuestas a uno de los muchos misterios del Universo. Más lejos que nunca . La FRB en cuestión se llama FRB 20240304B y fue detectada en primer lugar por el radiotelescopio MeerKAT, ubicado en Sudáfrica. Después, gracias al Telescopio Espacial James Webb, los… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Polyethylene Microplastics And Liver Risk: Texas A&M links exposure to fatty liver signs; questions remain for human health
item.description: New research from Texas A&M University indicates that polyethylene microplastics may affect liver health negatively. The study observed significant signs of fatty liver disease linked to polyethylene exposure and a high-fat diet. Researchers found changes in gene activity related to fat metabolism and tissue repair. Future investigations will focus on whether these pollutants contribute to more severe liver damage. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance rover breaks Mars driving record, covering 28.1 miles in five years
item.description: NASA's Perseverance rover has set a new distance record on Mars, traveling 28.10 miles in its mission, eclipsing the previous record of 28.06 miles set by Opportunity in nearly 15 years. This remarkable feat, achieved over five and a half years, showcases Perseverance's advanced autonomous navigation system as it investigates ancient geological structures and collects rock samples to enhance our scientific insights. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: China tests a Dune-like iron-harvesting crawler robot in the Taklamakan Desert
item.description: Chinese researchers have built a self-propelled crawler robot that harvests iron from sand and have tested the device in the dunes of the vast Taklamakan Desert – an area the size of Germany – in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. In Frank Herbert’s classic science fiction novel Dune, mobile factories traverse the sands of the fictional planet Arrakis to extract the drug melange, also known as “spice”. The real-world device similarly travels across the desert, extracting... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
item.description: A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
item.description: A promising new treatment for knee arthritis uses tiny, dissolvable particles to block abnormal blood vessels, easing inflammation and pain without joint replacement surgery. In a study of 194 patients, 80% experienced clinically meaningful pain relief lasting at least 12 months. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: $20m public liability insurance to rally in a park: how council red tape hinders the right to protest

item.description: What a cosmic coincidence! In today’s image, Mars joins the Beehive cluster below an auroral curtain and above a horizon of happy little trees near Lansjärv, Sweden. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Wild bobwhite quail spotted after habitat restoration project
item.description: Multiple coveys of wild bobwhite quail were recently sighted at the University of Tennessee's Ames AgResearch and Education Center, marking an encouraging milestone in an ongoing effort to restore habitat for the species at this historic bird dog field trial destination. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
item.description: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Black women in food industries face systemic roadblocks
item.description: Lilly Jan was perplexed and a little annoyed. Last year, Jan, an assistant teaching professor in the Cornell Nolan School of Hotel Administration in the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, was trying to collect information on food industry businesses owned by Black women. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
item.description: Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Simple cleaning steps could curb deadly fungal disease risks for Australia's wild reptiles
item.description: With spring underway and the weather warming, reptiles are on the move in suburbs, parks and scrubland across Australia. Snake catchers and wildlife caregivers are responding to calls for help, and reptile enthusiasts—known as "herpers"—are heading outdoors in search of their next sighting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
item.description: Scientists used artificial intelligence to uncover nearly 10,000 chemical reactions involved in transforming carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals, revealing crucial pathways that traditional models had missed. The discovery dramatically improved predictions of CO2 conversion and uncovered a surprising hydrogen reaction that could inspire more efficient catalysts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
item.description: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons. The researchers measured it in a layer of the semiconductor tungsten diselenide, just one atomic layer thick, using ultrashort laser pulses. The results have been published in the latest issue of the journal Nature Photonics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover 'D-rex', a giant fungus from Chinese forests whose unique lineage dates back 65 million years
item.description: Deep in the forests of Yunnan, China, scientists have discovered a "fungal giant" that challenges our understanding of how large fungi can become. The newly described species, Dianjunus rex, produces vertical fruiting bodies up to 50 cm (20 inches) high and weighing up to 2.2 kg (4.9 pounds)—the largest known within the phylum Ascomycota. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Isle of Wight fossil Europe's first known long-clawed megaraptoran dinosaur
item.description: A new species of dinosaur—a long-clawed predator the size of a large tiger—has been discovered by a UCL-led team from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight. The dinosaur, described in a new paper in the journal Royal Society Open Science, belongs to a group of agile, two-legged carnivores called megaraptorans and is the first of this group to be found in Europe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: People with a 'good ear' for sounds make better language learners, study suggests
item.description: People who are better at noticing fine details in sound—an ability known as auditory precision—can master the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners, a new study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
item.description: A newly identified 210-million-year-old dinosaur from Zimbabwe is helping scientists uncover a surprisingly distinct prehistoric ecosystem. The discovery suggests that ancient climate differences may have separated dinosaur populations across southern Africa, leading to unique species that challenge previous assumptions about their evolution. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
item.description: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power memories and logic circuits. However, a major goal in the field has been to find practical ways to control their motion with high precision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Patterned X-rays map 3D chemical structures faster with fewer measurements
item.description: Seeing inside an object is one thing; seeing exactly what it is made of, in three dimensions, is far more difficult. Now, researchers at Bar-Ilan University and collaborating institutions have developed a new X-ray imaging technique that can map the three-dimensional chemical composition of an object 43 times faster than conventional approaches, while using more than 97% less measurement data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Computational model guides lighting design to improve color discrimination in aging eyes
item.description: Researchers have developed a new computational model that accounts for the effects of aging on our eyes' ability to discriminate color. It could help guide lighting designs that make it easier for older adults to perceive colors while preserving the expected appearance for people with typical color vision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How eye-catching social media feeds steer attention toward misinformation
item.description: A research team led by Jiyoung Lee, a professor in the Department of Media and Communication, has worked with international researchers to uncover how visual contrast across social media feeds influences how quickly users spot visual misinformation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hawaiian coral tests reveal heat tolerance varies by species and location
item.description: As ocean temperatures rise, corals' ability to withstand and adapt to heat stress is critical for the future of coral reefs. Many reef-building corals already live near their upper thermal limits, making them vulnerable to bleaching and, with prolonged stress, mortality. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The politics of city rats: What urban rodents tell us about housing and sanitation
item.description: Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems. While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Thwaites Glacier could contribute twice as much sea-level rise as previously projected
item.description: A new ice sheet model developed by glaciologists at the University of California, Irvine and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory projects that the melting of Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica will contribute up to 30 millimeters (1.2 inches) of sea level rise by 2100—twice previous estimates—even without additional climate warming. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could meditation reveal an SU(3) symmetry shared by the observer and the universe?
item.description: You sit down to meditate. A conversation returns, then thoughts. You bring your attention back to the breath. Sometimes, after many such returns, the effort eases. Thoughts lose their urgency, while awareness remains clear. Less occupies the mind, yet the moment still feels whole. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drier Texas rivers support simpler food webs and higher animal productivity, study finds
item.description: Global warming is often treated as synonymous with climate change, but rising temperatures are only one consequence of the human-driven phenomenon. Changes in rainfall patterns are another, but their effects on ecosystems are less understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Carpet' growth method yields long-sought 2D quantum material
item.description: For decades, physicists have sought a practical two-dimensional topological insulator: an ultrathin material whose interior blocks electricity but whose edges conduct it. In ordinary wires, electrons constantly bounce off imperfections, losing energy. But along the edges of a 2D topological insulator, electrons with opposite spins travel in opposite directions, like cars in one-way lanes, so they rarely scatter and lose energy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Liquid metal dealloying creates nanoporous silicon carbide at just 800°C
item.description: Silicon carbide (SiC) is a ceramic known for its excellent heat resistance and chemical stability, which makes it attractive for a wide range of applications like electronics, catalysts and energy-related materials. However, SiC generally requires high-temperature processing, and simultaneously forming and controlling porous structures at the nanometer scale remains challenging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. The research was recently published in the journal ACS Central Science and has already garnered attention from other experts in the field. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New topological microscope tip reveals evidence of 2D altermagnetism
item.description: Researchers have fashioned a layered topological material into a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) tip that senses spin-related electronic states at atomic resolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: For decades, scientists have been able to look at individual moments in the development of an embryo: a snapshot of a developing brain, a picture of how the heart takes shape or a glimpse of cells beginning to form the nervous system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New method helps researchers study proteins involved in plant health, disease
item.description: Plants—like people—come in all shapes and sizes. And just like scientists want to understand the components of the human body to treat disease and improve our lives, they also want to understand how plants thrive, develop disease, succumb or survive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Humans and songbirds hear the same sounds, but organize them differently
item.description: Researchers from the University of Amsterdam and Leiden University have discovered that humans and songbirds use markedly different strategies to recognize sequences of complex sounds. The findings shed new light on how biology and experience shape the way we perceive complex sounds, with implications for music and speech. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21. item.title: Researchers uncover multiple genetic paths that lead to mottled feathers in chickens
item.description: The white-tipped feathers found in many chicken breeds may look like variations of the same decorative pattern, but new research shows that they do not all share the same genetic origin. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. This has resulted in two technologies that are widespread today: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is commonplace in hospitals, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is used to determine the structures of proteins and to develop new drugs. The mathematical framework of optimal control theory can be used to improve… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Researchers at the Oregon State University College of Science have developed a new electrochemical sensor for rapidly and accurately detecting a naturally occurring compound widely used in the food, beverage and fragrance industries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Want more women CEOs? Start with company structure, research finds
item.description: Women managers are significantly more likely to be promoted to CEO at companies organized into separate business units—each with its own revenues, costs and bottom line—than at companies that operate as a single, stand-alone entity, a new study led by the University of Massachusetts Amherst finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D map of rice development charts gene activity across plant's entire life cycle
item.description: Rice is one of the world's most familiar staple foods, but how does a single cell develop into a rice plant with specialized tissues and organs? A new study offers a detailed look at this process through a three-dimensional (3D) spatiotemporal atlas covering 10 organs and 61 developmental stages across the rice life cycle, from seed to seed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new way to replace carbon with nitrogen atoms could lead to better medicines
item.description: When drugmakers want to improve on compounds they have already created, they can replace a carbon atom with a nitrogen atom. While effective, the techniques they use to perform this chemical swap, known as skeletal editing, have some downsides. For example, older approaches often require harsh chemicals or only work on specific types of molecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Candida auris copies its entire genome to survive antifungal treatment, research reveals
item.description: New research has revealed an unexpected new mechanism through which the killer fungus Candida auris is resisting antifungal drug treatment. A team led by the University of Exeter and City St George's, University of London, discovered that the fungus creates multiple versions of its entire genome, including mutating a gene that plays a role in cell wall integrity, called "Crazy-one" (CRZ1). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite model finds Alpine peatlands may be smaller than official maps show
item.description: Peatlands in the Alps are mostly small, scattered and difficult to access. As a result, up-to-date information on their extent and condition is often lacking. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has now developed a cross-border approach to identifying these particular areas. A comparison with official maps shows that the model identifies many peatlands as smaller than previously mapped—particularly in areas where aerial photographs reveal visible signs of disturbance. The findings were published in the journal Communications Earth &… Fuente: Phys.org.
